To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) a clinical isolate of C. albicans with high-level azole resistance lacked the known mechanisms of resistance; 2) the azole resistance phenotype in this isolate was associated with increased expression of two drug efflux pumps; 3) a Chr4 tricopy contributed to azole-resistant phenotypes in the clinical isolate, but not in the standard SC5,314 laboratory strain background; 4) Chr6 trisomies did not contribute to azole resistance phenotypes

the presence of a trisomy of chromosome 4, but not chromosome 6, contributes to increased fluocazole resistance in a clinically relevant isolate of C. albicans, and that the presence of this trisomy has a greater impact in the P60002 background than in the commonly used SC5314 strain.
the presence of three chromosomes 4 (Chr 4) increases fluconazole resistance and that Chr 4 trisomies contribute to azole resistance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
identifying and characterizing the genetic determinants of fluconazole resistance.
understanding how the genetic background of a strain affects the expression of drug resistance phenotypes.

a Chr4 trismoy is associated with elevated fluconazole sensitivity in a C. albicans clinical isolate, and that this effect can only be observed in the P60002 genetic background.
